newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Growing Albania violence bodes ill for elections.
newsitem.headline: Growing Albania violence bodes ill for elections.

text.p: Growing violence in Albania, including a failed attempt on President Sali Berisha's life, is poisoning the run-up to this month's crucial early elections, Albanian and Western officials said on Thursday.

"It obviously makes things more difficult," Jeff Murray, spokesman for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation (OSCE), told Reuters after Albanian media reported that a man threw a dud hand grenade at Berisha during a campaign rally near Tirana.

"It doesn't improve the atmosphere for campaigning for the elections," Murray said, noting that the OSCE, which is providing monitors and technical assistance, still had no confirmation of what happened at the rally on Wednesday evening.
Albanian media said a man attending the rally at Shkallnuer, 40 km (25 miles) west of Tirana, threw a grenade that failed to explode.
The reported assassination attempt followed a Monday lunchtime blast that injured 20 people at a Tirana cafe frequented by followers of the Socialist Party, Berisha's main rivals.

Also this week, King Leka I, the pretender to the Albanian throne who has been campaigning for restoration of the monarchy in a referendum to coincide with the June 29 vote, was turned back from three towns by gunmen demanding he pay to enter.

And in the southern town of Berat, vigilantes killed two young men suspected of theft. Berat residents and newspaper reports said the men were beaten, tied up with barbed wire and dragged around the town by cars and later covered in petrol and set alight.

Murray said there was no immediate plan to delay the elections, called to restore stability to the turbulent Balkan state after widespread riots in March sparked by the collapse of dubious pyramid investment schemes. He said any change in the timetable would be up to the Albanian authorities.

"Whatever the animosities and lack of trust that exist, this has not been directed at the OSCE," he said. "Our belief is certainly at this point that the people understand we are here to try to help them restore civil society."

Namik Dokle, a senior leader of the Socialist Party, said the reported attack on Berisha "is a very harmful incident for the democratic breath which the political forces are trying to establish in Albania.
"But one wrong does not justify another -- battles can only be won by democratic means, with free and fair elections," he told Reuters.
He said one of the people most seriously injured in the Monday cafe bombing was a Socialist Party candidate who had to go abroad for treatment of eye wounds.

A Western diplomat said bombings were common in Albanian society and were used to send a strong message to, for example, judges or policemen, but that the violence that has swept the country since the March riots was getting out of hand.
"If it finally takes the horror of bombings and Colombia-style killings in the provinces to cause people to pull together and say 'that's enough,' I hope to God it happens," the diplomat said.
